title: Feature Selective Model Collapse in Diffusion Models: Total Replacement versus Fixed-Budget Training

paper.title: Feature Selective Model Collapse in Diffusion Models: Total Replacement versus Fixed-Budget Training
paper.abstract:
Abstract Model collapse arises when generative models are trained on synthetic data produced by earlier models. The phenomenon has attracted considerable attention because of its societal and technical implications. However, previous studies have reached seemingly contradictory conclusions: replacing real data with synthetic data causes collapse (Shumailov et al.), yet accumulating real data alongside synthetic data can prevent it. For diffusion models,
we study an intermediate regime typical of finite-budget pipelines: all past datasets and the real data are kept, but each new model is trained on a fixed-size sample from this growing pool, so the real fraction vanishes without any data being removed.
Experiments on a 2D spiral dataset as well as the image benchmarks (MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, and CIFAR-10) show that replacement protocol degrades dataset rapidly as in the literature, whereas the fixed budget degrades only partially, sparing some features. A linear-response model of the multi-generational parameter dynamics, analyzed by stochastic recursion, confirms that the two protocols differ: some features will be fragile and lost within a few generations for both protocols, while some will be robust and preserved over practically unbounded horizons under the fixed budget protocol.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Generative models are increasingly trained on data that already contains the output of earlier models. As synthetic content becomes ubiquitous and training pipelines rely on ever larger datasets collected over long periods of time, understanding the long-term consequences of such recursive training has become both a practical and a theoretical necessity with societal and technical implications. Shumailov et al. (2024) (see also Dohmatob et al. (2024b) ) showed that this feedback loop degrades successive models until the tails of the original distribution disappear, a phenomenon they called model collapse . Their main protocol is one of recursive replacement: each generation is trained on the output of the previous one, and the real dataset is gone after the first step. Subsequent work reached conclusions that appear to contradict this one. Gerstgrasser et al. (2024) argued that if synthetic data accumulate alongside the real data instead of replacing it collapse no longer occurs. Seddik et al. (2024) made collapse depend on the synthetic-to-real ratio rather than on the recursion itself, and Barzilai and Shamir (2026) showed that for maximum likelihood estimation collapse can be avoided even when the fraction of real data vanishes, while also exhibiting cases where it cannot. Zhu et al. (2025) approach the question from the mitigation side, editing human-produced text rather than regenerating it. Closer to us in model class, Yoon et al. (2025) and Bohacek and Farid (2025) document collapse in finetuned Stable Diffusion over short chains. We investigate a recursive-training protocol that is intermediate between those of Shumailov et al. (2024) and Gerstgrasser et al. (2024) . As in the latter, synthetic data are accumulated rather than replacing the original dataset. However, unlike that setting, here the training-set size is kept fixed: at each generation, a constant number of examples is resampled from the growing data pool. This regime, which naturally arises under a finite training budget, was introduced as accumulate-subsample by Kazdan et al. (2025) and examined empirically for diffusion models by Shi et al. (2025) ; we complement these works with a per-feature theoretical analysis. Our contributions are both empirical and theoretical. On the empirical side, we focus on the class of diffusion models that has received comparatively less attention in the model-collapse literature. We recursively train diffusion models over several generations, first on a toy 2D spiral distribution and then on MNIST, Fashion-MNIST & CIFAR-10. Under total replacement, we recover the rapid deterioration reported in previous work. Under accumulation with a fixed dataset size and constant training budget, the deterioration is only partial and affects specific features, leading to a behavior that differs both from complete collapse and from the bounded-error regime predicted under unbounded accumulation. On the theoretical side, we introduce a system of equations describing the multi-generational parameter dynamics of recursively trained diffusion models. Like Bertrand et al. (2024) , we linearize the retraining map in parameter space; unlike their stability analysis, which requires a large enough fraction of real data, our model covers a real fraction vanishing as 1 / ( n + 1 ) 1/(n+1) and a random re-initialization at each generation. Using stochastic analysis, we establish rigorous convergence results that explain both the rapid degradation observed under total replacement and, in the fixed-budget accumulation regime, the heterogeneous evolution of reconstruction quality across different features. We also derive per-feature halving times which shows that recursive training first eliminates ’fragile’ features providing thus quantitative guidance on when real-data refreshes and related mitigation measures become necessary. A detailed positioning relative to prior work is presented in Appendix A . In short, the works differ less about the recursion itself than about how the training set is built at each step; the fixed training-set size removes the vanishing-noise-share weighting on which the protective effect of accumulation relies.

sections.heading: 2 Methodology
sections.text: We train diffusion models with DDPM training ( Ho et al., 2020 ) and DDIM sampling ( Song et al., 2021 ) . See appendix for architecture details. Each model is trained on a dataset and results in a new model called a "generation". Let 𝒟 \mathcal{D} be the real dataset (also denoted 𝒟 0 \mathcal{D}_{0} ), d d the number of model parameters and let S n ∈ ℝ d S_{n}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} denote the generative model parameters at generation n n ; once S n S_{n} is obtained, a synthetic dataset of size n d n_{d} , denoted 𝒟 n \mathcal{D}_{n} , is sampled using the S n S_{n} as model parameters. Two data protocols are used: the last generation protocol where generation n + 1 n+1 is trained on 𝒟 n \mathcal{D}_{n} alone and the fixed budget protocol where generation n + 1 n+1 is trained on a sample of fixed size n d n_{d} drawn from the pool 𝒟 ∪ 𝒟 1 ∪ ⋯ ∪ 𝒟 n \mathcal{D}\cup\mathcal{D}_{1}\cup\cdots\cup\mathcal{D}_{n} ; the pool grows but the training set does not, so the probability that a training example is real decreases with n n although no data is ever discarded. This protocol can describe for instance the data accumulation on internet, each new model trains only on a part of available corpora. All models start from a set of parameters Z n Z_{n} sampled at random from some distribution ν \nu . As datasets we use a toy 2D spiral dataset and then MNIST, Fashion-MNIST & CIFAR-10. Parameters We use n d ∼ 10 4 n_{d}\sim 10^{4} samples, n e ​ p ​ o ​ c ​ h ​ s ∼ 100 − 1000 n_{epochs}\sim 100-1000 epochs and n g ​ e ​ n ∼ 20 − 100 n_{gen}\sim 20-100 generations, cf. Appedix for details. To sample from the model we use a Exponential Model average with parameter 0.8 0.8 that smooths model parameters. Metrics. To evaluate the model collapse for image datasets we use three metrics: Fréchet Inception Distance (FID), pixel-FID (same formula as FID but without using Inception features) and Wasserstein-2 metric, denoted 𝒲 2 \mathcal{W}_{2} at pixel level. For the simple 2D spiral dataset neither the Inception features nor the pixel-space Fréchet distance make sense so we use 𝒲 2 \mathcal{W}_{2} computed exactly by solving the discrete optimal transport problem; in this case the Fréchet distance is computed between the Gaussian approximations of the two clouds in ℝ 2 \mathbb{R}^{2} .

sections.heading: What the analysis contributes as principle.
sections.text: While the two protocols are usually compared through the speed of degradation, we place the difference at the per-feature dynamics and obtain theoretical results concerning the feature decay ( 11 )–( 12 ) which are coherent with the experiments in Section 6 . The apparently divergent conclusions of Shumailov et al. (2024) , Gerstgrasser et al. (2024) , Seddik et al. (2024) and Barzilai and Shamir (2026) can now be reconciled for the diffusion model settings. Why these regimes matter in practice. The fragile/robust partition identified theoretically explains which features are at risk. Fragile features are those associated in earlier work with the tails and low-density regions of the distribution (rare and under-represented cases). For anyone training on web-scale corpora that already contain generated content, this turns a diffuse concern into a concrete encouragement to enforce provenance tracking, synthetic-content disclosure, or refreshing the data with real examples. In general we hope these insights can help asses and mitigate the effects of model collapse by strengthening preferentially the ’fragile’ features. On the other hand, the existence of robust features helps explain why collapse in practice is often partial rather than total, potentially even creating a false sense of reassurance that the procedure remains healthy. Limitations. Our theory is a first-order, NTK-style linear response resting on assumptions that real recursive training meets only approximately, and the identification of the eigenvectors of M M with semantic attributes is an interpretation rather than a consequence of the model. Empirically, we retrain small models from scratch with unconditional DDIM sampling, without sweeping the budget size or curating the pool, and our metrics measure distributional distance only. See Appendix E for the additional discussion on the limitations.

sections.heading: 8 Conclusion
sections.text: We studied recursive diffusion models training in two regimes: total replacement ("last generation" protocol) and a "fixed budget" protocol where synthetic data accumulate but the training budget and dataset size stay fixed. This latter regime, introduced as accumulate-subsample by Kazdan et al. (2025) , is relevant for finite-budget pipelines. Empirically, on a 2D spiral and on image benchmarks (MNIST, Fashion-MNIST & CIFAR-10) degradation under a fixed budget is partial and feature-selective, unlike the general rapid collapse of pure replacement. Theoretically, we gave a linear-response framework for this setting, complementary to the stability analysis of Bertrand et al. (2024) , and show rigorously that the two protocols differ in kind, not degree, and the dataset characteristics split into fragile features, forgotten within a few generations, and robust features that a fixed budget preserves over practically unbounded horizons. For the principled study of generative modeling, this reconciles previously discordant results; for the trustworthy and sustainable use of these models, it provides a way to anticipate which content, especially the tails and under-represented, fragile, modes, is lost under recursive training on accumulating data, and how many generations that takes. Identifying features semantically, scaling to large pretrained models and conditional sampling, modeling curation of the pool, and relating halving times to explicit fairness criteria are the natural next steps.

sections.heading: Appendix A Related literature and positioning
sections.text: We recall below some of the works that documented model collapse. The works disagree less about the recursion itself than about how the training set is built at each step. Shumailov et al. (2024) test on VAE, GMM, and language models and refit each generation on a finite sample drawn from its predecessor, with no real data retained. We will call this protocol the "last generation" protocol. They distinguish an early phase, in which the low-probability regions of the distribution are lost, from a late phase, in which modes merge and the generated distribution concentrates on a point estimate, and they show that the finite sample size alone suffices to produce this, independently of any limitation in the expressivity of the model. We retain the finite per-generation sample, which is the mechanism they identify, but not the deletion of the real data. The three works of Dohmatob et al. (2024a) ; Dohmatob et al. (2024b) ; Dohmatob et al. (2025) analyze model collapse through tractable regression and generative models. They show that recursive training on synthetic data changes the relevant scaling laws, primarily because rare events and distributional tails are progressively lost, leading to bias, un-learning, and eventual collapse. While the first two works focus mainly on recursive self-training and also consider mixtures of real and synthetic data, Dohmatob et al. (2025) specifically studies a growing data set with a fixed nonzero synthetic proportion. It shows that performance may fail to improve, or may even collapse, as the total data size grows, since the synthetic fraction does not vanish. The first two works are therefore closest to our “last generation” protocol, whereas the latter provides a comparison with growing-data protocols. Gerstgrasser et al. (2024) discuss LLMs and generative language models in general and let the training set grow: generation n n is fit on the union of the real dataset and all previous synthetic generations. The protection they establish comes from this growth, since a generation that contributes a vanishing share of the training set also contributes a vanishing share of the noise. It is arguably not a consequence of the presence of the real data as such. We depart from it on one point: instead of training on the accumulated pool we only train on a fixed size sample from the generated pool. Note in particular that the fixed size removes the weighting that makes their argument work. Kazdan et al. (2025) introduce exactly our fixed budget protocol under the name accumulate-subsample , with the same finite-compute motivation, and report across five generative settings a test loss lying between those of replacement and accumulation and typically reaching a plateau. Our experiments are consistent with this picture. What we add is a per-feature account of it: the plateau reflects robust features, whose halving time grows as 2 1 / λ 2^{1/\lambda} , while fragile features are lost as fast as under replacement. Seddik et al. (2024) focus on LLM (autoregressive language models) and predict a threshold phenomenon, with a maximal proportion of synthetic data below which collapse is avoided, and show in the purely synthetic regime that the learned distribution converges to a point mass supported on an outcome that was likely under the original distribution. Because our protocol drives the real proportion to zero, their framework is the one that most directly predicts what we observe, and their tails-first ordering is the discrete counterpart of the feature-selective degradation reported in Section 6 . Barzilai and Shamir (2026) work with generic generative models under maximum likelihood estimation in an accumulating setting and avoid collapse even as the real fraction vanishes, but under two conditions that our setting does not meet: the number of samples drawn per generation must grow with the number of generations, whereas ours is constant, and the family of distributions must be smooth enough, failing which they construct consistent families that collapse arbitrarily fast. DDIM sampling has no maximum likelihood property to begin with, so their positive result does not transfer, while their negative results show that accumulation alone is not a guarantee. Bertrand et al. (2024) study likelihood-based generative models, diffusion models among them, retrained on a mixture of their own samples and a fixed proportion of the real data. They linearize the retraining map in parameter space around the optimum and prove stability when the initial model is accurate enough and the real proportion stays above a threshold. Our framework rests on the same kind of first-order linearization but differs in three respects: under the fixed budget the real proportion vanishes as 1 / ( n + 1 ) 1/(n+1) , so their threshold is eventually crossed; each generation is re-initialized at random, which is the source of the noise term M ​ Z n MZ_{n} ; and we derive per-feature halving times rather than a stability condition, which is what separates fragile from robust features. Applied to autoregressive transformers LLMs, Zhu et al. (2025) study mixtures of real and synthetic text at a fixed synthetic proportion rather than long recursive chains, and propose token-level editing of human-produced data as a remedy. Their observation that synthetic data cover only a narrowed portion of the original distribution is the language-model analogue of the loss of low-density features we report, obtained without any recursion at all. We now discuss three works that study diffusion models rather than language models. Yoon et al. (2025) finetune Stable Diffusion v1.5 with LoRA on its own outputs, restarting each iteration from the same pretrained weights on a fixed prompt set with no real data retained: a last generation protocol with a deterministic and strongly informative initialization. Their central finding is that the classifier-free guidance scale governs both the speed and the direction of degradation, low guidance producing blurring and high guidance high-frequency artifacts. This mechanism has no counterpart here, where sampling is unconditional, which is one reason our degradation is feature-selective rather than directional. Their quantitative-trait analysis yields a drifting mean with variance stabilizing at a positive value; Theorem 4.1 reaches a comparable non-degenerate limit through an unrelated mechanism. Bohacek and Farid (2025) retrain the denoising network of Stable Diffusion on faces of its own creation over five iterations, at fixed synthetic proportions from 3.3 % 3.3\% to 100 % 100\% . Collapse occurs at every proportion, and curation of the retraining set does not slow it down. Their real proportion stays constant across iterations rather than being driven to zero as in our fixed budget protocol, so their result bounds how little synthetic data suffices but leaves the long-horizon asymptotics open. Their healing experiment, where FID recovers while artifacts persist, indicates that part of the information survives the chain, consistent with the robust features of Section 5 . Both works finetune a large pretrained model over few iterations, whereas we retrain small models from scratch over one hundred generations, so the pretrained weights play in their setting the role that the random initialization Z n Z_{n} plays in ours. Shi et al. (2025) retrain DDPMs from scratch on CIFAR-10, FFHQ and MNIST under both replacement and accumulate-subsample, over fewer than ten iterations. They identify a transition from generalization to memorization driven by the decreasing entropy of the training set, and propose an entropy-based selection of the training subset as a remedy. Their study is empirical and measures sample novelty; ours follows the same protocol over one hundred generations and gives a theoretical account of which features survive. Recall on positioning. Our contributions are empirical and theoretical. Empirically, most model-collapse works study VAEs, GMMs or language models, while we work with diffusion models (DDPM training, DDIM sampling), which have received far less attention. Theoretically, we introduce a new vector-valued mathematical description of the multi-generational parameter dynamics and prove convergence results explaining both behaviors. In particular we recover the rapid collapse of total replacement but find that a fixed training budget causes only partial, feature-selective degradation.

sections.heading: Appendix E Detailed limitations
sections.text: • Modelling assumptions. The theory is a first-order, NTK-style linear response. It assumes an exact parameter representative for every dataset ( 1 ), linear interpolation in parameter space for data mixtures, a symmetric positive-definite contraction M M with a fixed spectrum, and centered i.i.d. noise and initialization independent across generations. Real recursive training meets none of these exactly; the remark after Theorem 4.2 only absorbs additive representation error. So it should be rather be read as the simplest linear model that can be relevant to this setting, not the most precise one. • Feature identification. The features are eigenvectors of M M . Their identification with semantic attributes of the data, or with distribution tails, is an interpretation supported by the experiments and by analogy with Seddik et al. (2024) , not something the model establishes. • Sampler and setting. We use unconditional DDIM sampling, which has no maximum-likelihood property, so the positive result of Barzilai and Shamir (2026) does not apply and ours does not transfer to guided or conditional generation, where Yoon et al. (2025) show the guidance scale drives degradation. • Scale. We retrain small models from scratch, with n d n_{d} samples on several datasets. The behavior of the fragile/robust partition for large pretrained models finetuned over few iterations ( Bohacek and Farid, 2025 ; Yoon et al., 2025 ) is not tested here. • Pipeline realism. We do not sweep the budget size or the pool-mixing ratio, and we do no model curation or filtering of the pool, which Bohacek and Farid (2025) report can change the picture. • Metrics. FID, pixel-FID and 𝒲 2 \mathcal{W}_{2} measure distributional distance, not downstream utility or any explicit fairness criterion; connecting halving times to the latter is left open.

sections.heading: F.1 Recursive training protocol.
sections.text: Generation 0 is trained from scratch on n d = 10 000 n_{d}=10\,000 real images (see Section G for 2D-spiral dataset). After training, the EMA model generates another n d n_{d} synthetic samples. For generation g > 0 g>0 , a pool is constructed from 𝒫 ​ o ​ o ​ l n = 𝒟 ∪ 𝒟 1 ∪ ⋯ ∪ 𝒟 n − 1 , \displaystyle\mathcal{P}ool_{n}=\mathcal{D}\cup\mathcal{D}_{1}\cup\dots\cup\mathcal{D}_{n-1}, (26) where 𝒟 n \mathcal{D}_{n} denotes the synthetic dataset produced at generation n n . The trained model then generates a new synthetic dataset 𝒟 n \mathcal{D}_{n} , which is added to the pool for the next generation. The phenomenon has attracted considerable attention because of its societal and technical implications. However, previous studies have reached seemingly contradictory conclusions: replacing real data with synthetic data causes collapse (Shumailov et al.), yet accumulating real data alongside synthetic data can prevent it. For diffusion models, we study an intermediate regime typical of finite-budget pipelines: all past datasets and the real data are kept, but each new model is trained on a fixed-size sample from this growing pool, so the real fraction vanishes without any data being removed. Experiments on a 2D spiral dataset as well as the image benchmarks (MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, and CIFAR-10) show that replacement protocol degrades dataset rapidly as in the literature, whereas the fixed budget degrades only partially, sparing some features. A linear-response model of the multi-generational parameter dynamics, analyzed by stochastic recursion, confirms that the two protocols differ: some features will be fragile and lost within a few generations for both protocols, while some will be robust and preserved over practically unbounded horizons under the fixed budget protocol. 1 Introduction Generative models are increasingly trained on data that already contains the output of earlier models. As synthetic content becomes ubiquitous and training pipelines rely on ever larger datasets collected over long periods of time, understanding the long-term consequences of such recursive training has become both a practical and a theoretical necessity with societal and technical implications. Shumailov et al. (2024) (see also Dohmatob et al. (2024b) ) showed that this feedback loop degrades successive models until the tails of the original distribution disappear, a phenomenon they called model collapse . Their main protocol is one of recursive replacement: each generation is trained on the output of the previous one, and the real dataset is gone after the first step. Subsequent work reached conclusions that appear to contradict this one. Gerstgrasser et al. (2024) argued that if synthetic data accumulate alongside the real data instead of replacing it collapse no longer occurs. Seddik et al. (2024) made collapse depend on the synthetic-to-real ratio rather than on the recursion itself, and Barzilai and Shamir (2026) showed that for maximum likelihood estimation collapse can be avoided even when the fraction of real data vanishes, while also exhibiting cases where it cannot. Zhu et al. (2025) approach the question from the mitigation side, editing human-produced text rather than regenerating it. Closer to us in model class, Yoon et al. (2025) and Bohacek and Farid (2025) document collapse in finetuned Stable Diffusion over short chains. We investigate a recursive-training protocol that is intermediate between those of Shumailov et al. (2024) and Gerstgrasser et al. (2024) . As in the latter, synthetic data are accumulated rather than replacing the original dataset. However, unlike that setting, here the training-set size is kept fixed: at each generation, a constant number of examples is resampled from the growing data pool. This regime, which naturally arises under a finite training budget, was introduced as accumulate-subsample by Kazdan et al. (2025) and examined empirically for diffusion models by Shi et al. (2025) ; we complement these works with a per-feature theoretical analysis. Our contributions are both empirical and theoretical. On the empirical side, we focus on the class of diffusion models that has received comparatively less attention in the model-collapse literature. We recursively train diffusion models over several generations, first on a toy 2D spiral distribution and then on MNIST, Fashion-MNIST & CIFAR-10. Under total replacement, we recover the rapid deterioration reported in previous work. Under accumulation with a fixed dataset size and constant training budget, the deterioration is only partial and affects specific features, leading to a behavior that differs both from complete collapse and from the bounded-error regime predicted under unbounded accumulation. On the theoretical side, we introduce a system of equations describing the multi-generational parameter dynamics of recursively trained diffusion models. Like Bertrand et al. (2024) , we linearize the retraining map in parameter space; unlike their stability analysis, which requires a large enough fraction of real data, our model covers a real fraction vanishing as 1 / ( n + 1 ) 1/(n+1) and a random re-initialization at each generation. Using stochastic analysis, we establish rigorous convergence results that explain both the rapid degradation observed under total replacement and, in the fixed-budget accumulation regime, the heterogeneous evolution of reconstruction quality across different features. We also derive per-feature halving times which shows that recursive training first eliminates ’fragile’ features providing thus quantitative guidance on when real-data refreshes and related mitigation measures become necessary. A detailed positioning relative to prior work is presented in Appendix A . In short, the works differ less about the recursion itself than about how the training set is built at each step; the fixed training-set size removes the vanishing-noise-share weighting on which the protective effect of accumulation relies. 2 Methodology We train diffusion models with DDPM training ( Ho et al., 2020 ) and DDIM sampling ( Song et al., 2021 ) . See appendix for architecture details. Each model is trained on a dataset and results in a new model called a "generation". Let 𝒟 \mathcal{D} be the real dataset (also denoted 𝒟 0 \mathcal{D}_{0} ), d d the number of model parameters and let S n ∈ ℝ d S_{n}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} denote the generative model parameters at generation n n ; once S n S_{n} is obtained, a synthetic dataset of size n d n_{d} , denoted 𝒟 n \mathcal{D}_{n} , is sampled using the S n S_{n} as model parameters. Two data protocols are used: the last generation protocol where generation n + 1 n+1 is trained on 𝒟 n \mathcal{D}_{n} alone and the fixed budget protocol where generation n + 1 n+1 is trained on a sample of fixed size n d n_{d} drawn from the pool 𝒟 ∪ 𝒟 1 ∪ ⋯ ∪ 𝒟 n \mathcal{D}\cup\mathcal{D}_{1}\cup\cdots\cup\mathcal{D}_{n} ; the pool grows but the training set does not, so the probability that a training example is real decreases with n n although no data is ever discarded. This protocol can describe for instance the data accumulation on internet, each new model trains only on a part of available corpora. All models start from a set of parameters Z n Z_{n} sampled at random from some distribution ν \nu . As datasets we use a toy 2D spiral dataset and then MNIST, Fashion-MNIST & CIFAR-10. Parameters We use n d ∼ 10 4 n_{d}\sim 10^{4} samples, n e ​ p ​ o ​ c ​ h ​ s ∼ 100 − 1000 n_{epochs}\sim 100-1000 epochs and n g ​ e ​ n ∼ 20 − 100 n_{gen}\sim 20-100 generations, cf. While the two protocols are usually compared through the speed of degradation, we place the difference at the per-feature dynamics and obtain theoretical results concerning the feature decay ( 11 )–( 12 ) which are coherent with the experiments in Section 6 . The apparently divergent conclusions of Shumailov et al. (2024) , Gerstgrasser et al. (2024) , Seddik et al. (2024) and Barzilai and Shamir (2026) can now be reconciled for the diffusion model settings. Why these regimes matter in practice. The fragile/robust partition identified theoretically explains which features are at risk. Fragile features are those associated in earlier work with the tails and low-density regions of the distribution (rare and under-represented cases). For anyone training on web-scale corpora that already contain generated content, this turns a diffuse concern into a concrete encouragement to enforce provenance tracking, synthetic-content disclosure, or refreshing the data with real examples. In general we hope these insights can help asses and mitigate the effects of model collapse by strengthening preferentially the ’fragile’ features. On the other hand, the existence of robust features helps explain why collapse in practice is often partial rather than total, potentially even creating a false sense of reassurance that the procedure remains healthy. Limitations. Our theory is a first-order, NTK-style linear response resting on assumptions that real recursive training meets only approximately, and the identification of the eigenvectors of M M with semantic attributes is an interpretation rather than a consequence of the model. Empirically, we retrain small models from scratch with unconditional DDIM sampling, without sweeping the budget size or curating the pool, and our metrics measure distributional distance only. See Appendix E for the additional discussion on the limitations. 8 Conclusion We studied recursive diffusion models training in two regimes: total replacement ("last generation" protocol) and a "fixed budget" protocol where synthetic data accumulate but the training budget and dataset size stay fixed. This latter regime, introduced as accumulate-subsample by Kazdan et al. (2025) , is relevant for finite-budget pipelines. Empirically, on a 2D spiral and on image benchmarks (MNIST, Fashion-MNIST & CIFAR-10) degradation under a fixed budget is partial and feature-selective, unlike the general rapid collapse of pure replacement. Theoretically, we gave a linear-response framework for this setting, complementary to the stability analysis of Bertrand et al. (2024) , and show rigorously that the two protocols differ in kind, not degree, and the dataset characteristics split into fragile features, forgotten within a few generations, and robust features that a fixed budget preserves over practically unbounded horizons. For the principled study of generative modeling, this reconciles previously discordant results; for the trustworthy and sustainable use of these models, it provides a way to anticipate which content, especially the tails and under-represented, fragile, modes, is lost under recursive training on accumulating data, and how many generations that takes. Identifying features semantically, scaling to large pretrained models and conditional sampling, modeling curation of the pool, and relating halving times to explicit fairness criteria are the natural next steps. Appendix A Related literature and positioning We recall below some of the works that documented model collapse. The works disagree less about the recursion itself than about how the training set is built at each step. Shumailov et al. (2024) test on VAE, GMM, and language models and refit each generation on a finite sample drawn from its predecessor, with no real data retained. We will call this protocol the "last generation" protocol. They distinguish an early phase, in which the low-probability regions of the distribution are lost, from a late phase, in which modes merge and the generated distribution concentrates on a point estimate, and they show that the finite sample size alone suffices to produce this, independently of any limitation in the expressivity of the model. We retain the finite per-generation sample, which is the mechanism they identify, but not the deletion of the real data. The three works of Dohmatob et al. (2024a) ; Dohmatob et al. (2024b) ; Dohmatob et al. (2025) analyze model collapse through tractable regression and generative models. They show that recursive training on synthetic data changes the relevant scaling laws, primarily because rare events and distributional tails are progressively lost, leading to bias, un-learning, and eventual collapse. While the first two works focus mainly on recursive self-training and also consider mixtures of real and synthetic data, Dohmatob et al. (2025) specifically studies a growing data set with a fixed nonzero synthetic proportion. It shows that performance may fail to improve, or may even collapse, as the total data size grows, since the synthetic fraction does not vanish. The first two works are therefore closest to our “last generation” protocol, whereas the latter provides a comparison with growing-data protocols. Gerstgrasser et al. (2024) discuss LLMs and generative language models in general and let the training set grow: generation n n is fit on the union of the real dataset and all previous synthetic generations. The protection they establish comes from this growth, since a generation that contributes a vanishing share of the training set also contributes a vanishing share of the noise. It is arguably not a consequence of the presence of the real data as such. We depart from it on one point: instead of training on the accumulated pool we only train on a fixed size sample from the generated pool. Note in particular that the fixed size removes the weighting that makes their argument work. Kazdan et al. (2025) introduce exactly our fixed budget protocol under the name accumulate-subsample , with the same finite-compute motivation, and report across five generative settings a test loss lying between those of replacement and accumulation and typically reaching a plateau. Our experiments are consistent with this picture. What we add is a per-feature account of it: the plateau reflects robust features, whose halving time grows as 2 1 / λ 2^{1/\lambda} , while fragile features are lost as fast as under replacement. Seddik et al. (2024) focus on LLM (autoregressive language models) and predict a threshold phenomenon, with a maximal proportion of synthetic data below which collapse is avoided, and show in the purely synthetic regime that the learned distribution converges to a point mass supported on an outcome that was likely under the original distribution. Because our protocol drives the real proportion to zero, their framework is the one that most directly predicts what we observe, and their tails-first ordering is the discrete counterpart of the feature-selective degradation reported in Section 6 . Barzilai and Shamir (2026) work with generic generative models under maximum likelihood estimation in an accumulating setting and avoid collapse even as the real fraction vanishes, but under two conditions that our setting does not meet: the number of samples drawn per generation must grow with the number of generations, whereas ours is constant, and the family of distributions must be smooth enough, failing which they construct consistent families that collapse arbitrarily fast. DDIM sampling has no maximum likelihood property to begin with, so their positive result does not transfer, while their negative results show that accumulation alone is not a guarantee. Bertrand et al. (2024) study likelihood-based generative models, diffusion models among them, retrained on a mixture of their own samples and a fixed proportion of the real data. They linearize the retraining map in parameter space around the optimum and prove stability when the initial model is accurate enough and the real proportion stays above a threshold. Our framework rests on the same kind of first-order linearization but differs in three respects: under the fixed budget the real proportion vanishes as 1 / ( n + 1 ) 1/(n+1) , so their threshold is eventually crossed; each generation is re-initialized at random, which is the source of the noise term M ​ Z n MZ_{n} ; and we derive per-feature halving times rather than a stability condition, which is what separates fragile from robust features. Applied to autoregressive transformers LLMs, Zhu et al. (2025) study mixtures of real and synthetic text at a fixed synthetic proportion rather than long recursive chains, and propose token-level editing of human-produced data as a remedy. Their observation that synthetic data cover only a narrowed portion of the original distribution is the language-model analogue of the loss of low-density features we report, obtained without any recursion at all. Their central finding is that the classifier-free guidance scale governs both the speed and the direction of degradation, low guidance producing blurring and high guidance high-frequency artifacts. This mechanism has no counterpart here, where sampling is unconditional, which is one reason our degradation is feature-selective rather than directional. Their quantitative-trait analysis yields a drifting mean with variance stabilizing at a positive value; Theorem 4.1 reaches a comparable non-degenerate limit through an unrelated mechanism.
